description: We are a team of coding terminators. Rumor has it we don't need sleep and feed exclusively on complex problems to solve, which we devour like hot pizza, producing excellent and fail-proof code in return. Our combined tech knowledge and passion for computer science are probably on the level of University of Technology professors.
summary: We built a tool for digging through NASA experiment data. Raw files in awkward formats (TSV tables, Excel workbooks, PDF reports, nested folders of measurements) get cleaned up and turned into a searchable catalogue of datasets, events and projects. A Python backend serves that catalogue through an API. You can search it, filter it, open a single record, or ask for the nearest neighbours of an item to find similar experiments. A few special cases get their own endpoints, the main one being the SAFFIRE-3 spacecraft fire experiment. You can also type a filter in plain language, and a language model turns it into structured filters. The same model can write a short summary of a special case. Alongside the app there are Polars scripts for the heavier analysis: atmosphere and telemetry data, charts, scatter plots, and parameter sweeps, including one that proposes fuel candidates. A separate frontend sits on top of the API so people can browse and compare everything without touching the code.
details: Our project is a search and analysis tool for NASA's microgravity combustion experiments (ACME, BASS, CFI, SAFFIRE and others). The raw data is scattered across TSV files, Excel workbooks, PDF reports and nested folders. We turned all of it into one searchable catalogue. You can filter experiments, open a single record, and find the nearest neighbours of an experiment to see which others are similar. A few special cases, such as the SAFFIRE-3 spacecraft fire test, get their own detailed views. You can also type a filter in plain language, and an AI model converts it into structured filters. The same model can summarize a case in a few sentences. The benefit is time: normally a researcher would have to open dozens of differently formatted files to compare two experiments, and here that takes a few clicks. We want this to lower the barrier to reusing NASA's data, so that students and engineers who aren't combustion specialists can still explore it, which could help with fire-safety work and with planning future experiments in space. We built the backend in Python with FastAPI and Uvicorn, used Polars for data analysis and charts, pypdf to extract text from PDFs, the Anthropic API for the AI features, and jsonschema to validate the model's structured output. The frontend uses React 19, React Router and Vite, tested with Vitest. The creative parts are the nearest-neighbour search across very different experiments, the plain-language filtering, and the way we merged formats that were never meant to work together, plus a parameter sweep that proposes fuel candidates. Our main considerations were data quality, since the files are inconsistent, validating AI output so it can't invent filters, keeping the app fast on large tables, and keeping the interface simple for non-experts.
